It is called a glass-lung, though nothing on its world has a name for it.

It stands about the height of a person when it uncurls, but it is not upright in the way we are. Its body is a loose coil of translucent plates, stacked like wet slate and joined by pale cords of muscle that show through the skin. The plates are not armor. They are living crystal, grown from minerals dissolved out of the rain, and they flex with a dry, musical click when the creature breathes. Under them, light travels in slow pulses: blue when it is resting, a sickly amber when it is hungry.

Where a head might be, there is a cluster of six hollow stalks. Each ends in a dark pit lined with fine hairs that taste the air. It has no eyes. The stalks lean toward warmth, toward the metal-salt scent of its prey, toward the low vibration of stone shifting underfoot. A mouth sits lower, a vertical split in the coil that irises open into a ring of glassy teeth. It does not chew. It presses the ring against a carcass and draws the soft parts inward in a single, patient swallow.

Its world is a twilight plain of black sand under a sky the color of bruised fruit. The sun is a dim red coal, and water falls as a thin, bitter mist rather than rain. Glass-lungs live in the hollows where that mist pools and freezes into needles at night. By day they burrow just under the sand, plates closed, stalking the heat that leaks from buried vents. At dusk they rise.

They do not hunt alone, and they do not hunt in packs the way wolves do. Three or four will settle in a loose ring around a vent and wait, each one still enough that drifting sand skins over its plates and hides the glow. When something warm crosses the circle—a low, six-legged grazer with a hide like cracked leather—they do not chase. They sing. The plates vibrate at a pitch the grazer feels in its joints, a note that makes the legs lock. Then the nearest glass-lung opens, and the others close in only after the first has fed. They share by leaving, not by fighting. A glass-lung that takes too much is left outside the ring the next dusk, and alone it starves, because the grazers will not freeze for a single voice.

They breed once in a long year, when the mist thickens and the vents steam harder. Two coil together until their plates interlock. Over days, a third set of plates grows between them, cloudy and soft. When it hardens, the parents uncouple and abandon it in the sand. The young one does not move for a season. It drinks the mist through its skin and grows its stalks in the dark. The first time it rises, it has no song of its own. It must find a ring and learn the note by lying still among the adults until its plates remember the pitch.

They do not build. They do not keep young. A glass-lung’s whole life is the ring, the mist, the slow amber pulse under the plates, and the moment the grazer’s legs go still. When one dies, the others do not notice except as a gap in the song. Sand covers the plates by morning. By the next dusk, the crystal has already begun to cloud and crack, returning its minerals to the bitter rain.

The creature is a silt-weaver from a dim, tidally locked world where a shallow ocean never freezes and never truly boils—only steams where the day side meets the night.

When something approaches, the pits flush violet and the whole rim lifts, turning the creature into a shallow cup. Sound, such as it is, travels through the water as pressure; the silt-weaver “hears” by letting its fringe flutter, then stilling the strands that match an incoming wave.

Locomotion is a crawl and a drift. On the bottom it ripples its underside against the silt, leaving a braided track. In open water it inflates a thin gas bladder grown from the same slime it weaves, rises a few body-lengths, and lets the slow current carry it until the bladder collapses and it sinks again. It never swims hard. Energy is scarce, and almost everything it does is a way of spending less of it.

**The Veil-Lantern of Kaeris**

On Kaeris, a tide-locked world of black basalt and pale ammonia seas, the dominant animal is the veil-lantern: a floating colony creature about the size of a horse when fully expanded, though it has no bones and no fixed outline.

Its body is a translucent sac the color of storm clouds, shot through with branching veins of coppery orange. Those veins are not blood. They are living filaments that carry mineral salts and harvest light. Embedded in the sac are clusters of glassy nodules—some clear, some the deep violet of old ink. When the creature feeds or signals, the nodules brighten until the whole animal looks like a lantern seen through fog. That glow is chemical, not fire: a slow reaction between compounds in the nodules and the thin, hydrogen-rich air.

A fringe of ribbon-like “veils” hangs from the underside. Each ribbon is edged with microscopic hooks that snag drifting ice crystals and the protein-rich spores that blow off the planet’s pale fungal plains. The veils also steer. By stiffening one side and slackening the other, the lantern tilts, catches the constant wind that races from the hot dayside toward the frozen night, and glides without ever touching the ground. It never lands if it can help it. The surface is too cold, and the ammonia pools dissolve the outer membrane if contact lasts more than a few minutes.

Inside the sac live three kinds of partners, none of them parasites in the usual sense. One is a threadlike microbe that fixes nitrogen from the air and shares it with the host. Another is a slow-growing crystal colony that stores energy as layered mineral sheets; in long darkness the lantern slowly dissolves those sheets and lives on the heat and chemistry they release. The third is a swarm of pinhead organisms that patrol the inner wall and seal punctures with a sticky resin. A single veil-lantern is really a moving pact among these four lives.

They reproduce by fission after a storm. When wind shear tears a mature lantern almost in two, the halves seal themselves, each taking a share of the nodules, the crystal stores, and the microbial partners. For a few days the new pair drifts in formation, exchanging faint pulses of light—possibly a way of matching internal chemistry before they separate for good. Young lanterns are nearly clear and clumsy; their veils are short, and they hug the warmer updrafts above the fungal plains until their nodules darken and their glow steadies.

They have no eyes and no brain in any Earth sense. A net of pressure-sensitive cells across the sac reads the wind, and the nodules themselves react to certain wavelengths, brightening when another lantern is near. Herds of dozens sometimes gather above a spore bloom, their lights pulsing in loose rhythm, not quite language and not quite reflex. When a razor-kite—Kaeris’s only true predator, a flat glider with acid-edged wings—cuts through the herd, the lanterns dim at once and drop lower, veils furled, until they look like scraps of cloud. Most escape. A few do not. What remains of a killed lantern freezes into a delicate lattice that the wind eventually grinds into mineral dust, which the plains later drink.

They live for decades if the storms are kind, always moving, always slightly luminous, never quite solid—creatures built for a world where the ground is a hazard and the sky is home.
